'''George "G." Michael Bancroft''', {{Post-nominals|country=CAN|OC|FRSC}}, (born 1942) is a Canadian [[chemist]] and [[emeritus professor]] at the [[University of Western Ontario]]. One of the world's leading experts in [[Mössbauer spectroscopy]],<ref name="Tribute" /> he is also known as one of the driving forces behind the development of [[synchrotron]] science in Canada,<ref name="Tribute" /> becoming the first director of the [[Canadian Light Source]] synchrotron after a 30-year "Odyssey".<ref name="Bancroft" />

==Early life and education==
Bancroft was born in [[Saskatoon, Saskatchewan]], the son of an accountant, but grew up in [[Winnipeg, Manitoba]]<ref name="Biography" /> where he attended [[Kelvin High School]].<ref>[https://www.facebook.com/photo.php?pid=950773&l=7c8e41bbe3&id=197714886941126 Kelvin High 100th anniversary]</ref>   
He graduated from the [[University of Manitoba]] in 1963, subsequently earning an MSc in chemistry (1964) from the same institution. Later that year he went to the [[University of Cambridge]], England to study for a PhD at [[Corpus Christi College, Cambridge|Corpus Christi College]]. He worked under the supervision of A.G. Maddock on the development of [[Mössbauer spectroscopy]], obtaining his PhD in 1967.<ref name="Biography">{{Cite journal|date=2007|title=Biography|journal=Canadian Journal of Chemistry|volume=85 |pages=xiii|doi=10.1139/v07-907}}</ref> Over a 20-year period Bancroft would become one of the world's leading experts in Mössbauer spectroscopy, publishing more than 80 papers, a major review and an authoritative textbook in the field.<ref name="Tribute">{{Cite journal|last=Carty |first=Arthur|date=2007|title=Tribute|journal=Canadian Journal of Chemistry|volume=85 |pages=xv-xix|doi=10.1139/v07-909}}</ref>

==University of Western Ontario==
After working as a [[postdoctoral research|postdoc]] at the University of Manitoba, Bancroft returned to Cambridge as a [[Fellow]] at [[Christ's College, Cambridge|Christ's College]].

Bancroft returned to Canada in 1970, as an [[assistant professor]] in the department of [[chemistry]] at the University of Western Ontario (UWO), becoming a [[professor]] in 1974, spending two periods as head of department. Bancroft was director of the Centre for Chemical Physics from 1977 to 1981, establishing Surface Science Western during his tenure.<ref name="Biography" /> At UWO Bancroft became interested in [[photoemission spectroscopy]], and in 1972, with [[National Research Council (Canada)|National Research Council]] (NRC) support, a spectrometer was purchased for research using far [[ultraviolet]] and [[X-ray]] [[photon]]s. This purchase also involved the universities of [[University of Toronto|Toronto]] and [[University of Windsor|Windsor]] in a Southwestern [[Ontario]] consortium.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.innovation.ca/AboutUs/Publicationsandreports/innovation/SynchrotronRadiationMostVersatileSpectroscopicSource|title=Synchrotron Radiation: The Most Versatile Spectroscopic Source|access-date=2012-07-29|archive-date=2015-10-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151023154010/http://www.innovation.ca/AboutUs/Publicationsandreports/innovation/SynchrotronRadiationMostVersatileSpectroscopicSource|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Canadian Synchrotron Radiation Facility==
{{main|Canadian Synchrotron Radiation Facility}}
In 1972 Bancroft took part in a workshop organised by Bill McGowan of (UWO) on the uses of [[synchrotron radiation]], an event he has described "the beginning of my 30 year odyssey to develop Canadian synchrotron capabilities in the US and then in Canada". He began work at the [[Synchrotron Radiation Center]] (SRC) at the [[University of Wisconsin-Madison]], US, in 1975, as a result of contact established with then-SRC director Ed Rowe at the 1972 meeting. After several failed attempts were made to establish a synchrotron facility in Canada, Bancroft submitted a proposal to the NRC to build a Canadian [[beamline]] at SRC. In 1978 the newly created [[Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council|NSERC]] awarded capital funding, and the Canadian Synchrotron Radiation Facility (CSRF) was founded. CSRF, owned and operated by NRC, with Bancroft as scientific director, grew from the initial beamline to a total of three by 1998.<ref name="Bancroft" />

==Canadian Light Source==
{{main|Canadian Light Source}}
The push for a synchrotron lightsource in Canada gained impetus in the early 1990s with the formation of the Canadian Institute for Synchrotron Radiation (CISR) with Bancroft as president. In 1994 NSERC recommended building a Canadian synchrotron, and set up a committee to decide between two rival bids to host the facility, led by Dennis Skopik of the [[University of Saskatchewan]] and Bancroft of UWO. In 1996 the committee recommend that the Canadian Light Source (CLS) be built in Saskatoon.
With the formation of the [[Canada Foundation for Innovation]] a funding mechanism for the lightsource became available, and after what Bancroft has described as a "Herculean" effort by the Saskatchewan team the funding was finalised in 1999. At this point Skopik departed to the US, and Bancroft was appointed as the first director of the CLS.<ref name="Bancroft">{{Cite journal
 |last=Bancroft |first=G. M.
 |date=2004
 |title=The Canadian Light Source – History and scientific prospects
 |journal=Canadian Journal of Chemistry
 |volume=82 |pages=1028–1042
 |doi=10.1139/v04-027
}}</ref> 
Bancroft's appointment ended in 2001,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.lightsource.ca/enews/newsletter_October2001.php |title=CLS Newsletter October 2001 |access-date=2012-07-28 |archive-date=2012-02-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120204083647/http://www.lightsource.ca/enews/newsletter_October2001.php |url-status=dead }}</ref>  although he remained as research director until 2004,<ref name="award">{{cite web|url=http://www.lightsource.ca/uso/bancroftthesisaward.php|title=G. Michael Bancroft Ph.D. Thesis Award|access-date=2012-07-28|archive-date=2012-08-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120809014755/http://www.lightsource.ca/uso/bancroftthesisaward.php|url-status=dead}}</ref> and he returned to UWO. Bancroft's association with the CLS continues, and he currently serves on their board of directors.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.lightsource.ca/aboutus/board.php|title=Board of Directors|access-date=2012-07-28}}{{Dead link|date=July 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

==Awards and honours==
Bancroft was elected as a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Canada]] (RSC) in 1979 (at the age of 37),<ref name="Tribute" /> and was inducted into the [[Order of Canada]] in 2003.<ref name="OOC">{{cite web|url=https://www.gg.ca/en/honours/recipients/146-8449|title=Mr. G. Michael Bancroft|date= 15 December 2003|publisher=[[Governor General of Canada]]|access-date=17 April 2021}}</ref>
He was awarded the RSC's [[Rutherford Memorial Medal]] in 1980, a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] in 1982/3, and the CIC and Montreal medals of the [[Chemical Institute of Canada]] in 1996 and 2002 respectively.<ref name="Tribute" /> The Canadian Light Source annual award for best PhD thesis is named for Bancroft.<ref name="award" />
